lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Real Complaint
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Vitor (Mock Communicative) | Lesson 1 -- The Real Complaint

listenings.text: Welcome back to Front Desk, the podcast for people who run hotels. Today I want to tell you about the most useful complaint I ever received, because it changed how I train every person at my reception desk. A guest came down at eleven at night and told me the room was unacceptable. Her exact word. Unacceptable. Now, my first instinct was to defend the room, because I had checked that room myself that afternoon and there was nothing wrong with it. But I have learned something over fifteen years in this job: the first complaint is almost never the real one. It is just the one that is easiest to say out loud at eleven at night. So instead of explaining, I asked one question. I said, what happened tonight? And she told me. She had a video call with her team in Singapore at nine, and the internet dropped four times. She missed the call. By the time she came downstairs, the room had become the enemy, because the room was the only thing in the building she could point at. The internet was the problem. The room was just the messenger. Here is what I did, and here is why. I did not apologise for the room, because the room was fine and she knew it. An apology for the wrong thing tells the guest you were not listening. I apologised for the call she missed. Then I moved her to a room on the second floor, where the signal is strongest, and I gave her the direct number of our night technician so she would not have to come downstairs again. She wrote to me two months later to book the same week. So my advice to you is this. When a guest complains, do not solve the sentence they said. Find the sentence they did not say. Ask what happened, listen to the whole answer without preparing your defence while they speak, and only then decide what to offer. It takes ninety seconds longer, and it saves the guest.

post_skill.title: What do you think?
items: "The room was just the messenger." What does she mean by that?
Do you agree that the first complaint is almost never the real one? Does that match your experience?
She apologised for the call, not for the room. Was that the right call, or is it a risk?
In your hotel, what is the complaint that is usually hiding something else?
Is there a moment when you SHOULD defend your hotel instead of digging deeper?

language.label: Target language — all of it came out of the recording
items: What happened tonight?
Tell me what happened.
Just so I understand correctly...
So the problem started on Monday?
I completely understand why you feel that way.
That would frustrate me too.
What I can offer is...
What would work best for you?
Would it help if...?
I'm afraid that's not something I can do, but...
I'll take care of it personally.
Leave it with me.

language.title: Six of them do six different jobs. Match each line to its job.
words: "I completely understand why you feel that way."
"Would it help if I moved you upstairs?"
defs: validates the feeling without admitting fault
tests a solution without promising it

language.text: Notice what is missing from the whole bank: the word "sorry" on its own. Every line either asks, validates, offers or owns. An apology with nothing after it leaves the guest exactly where they were.

pre_comm.title: Reveal answer key
list: Just so I understand correctly, the problem started on Monday?
I completely understand why you feel that way. Tell me what happened.
What I can offer is two nights, and I can do that now.
Would it help if I moved you to the second floor?
I'm afraid that's not something I can do, but I can hold your room until two.
I'll take care of it personally.
pre_comm.note: Accept justified variations. After each one, say it out loud: which sounds more natural in your voice?

items: The setup
Your teacher is Claire, a guest who has just come down to reception at 10pm. She says the room is unacceptable. That is all she will say at first.
Information gap
Claire answers ONLY as Claire, and only what you ask. She will not volunteer the real problem. Your job is to find it by talking to her — not by guessing.
Your goal
Leave the conversation knowing (1) what actually happened, (2) what she needs tonight, and (3) what you offered. Do not offer anything before you know the first two.

The situation

Different task, same theme. You are writing the complaint policy for your front desk team. Four real cases from last month are on the table. For each one you decide — compensate, apologise only, escalate, or refuse — and you say why out loud.

items.situation: A guest says the breakfast was cold. He ate all of it and complained at checkout, three days later.
tips: Does the delay change what you owe him?
What would you tell your team to do next time?

items.situation: A guest missed her flight because the wake-up call never came. Your system shows the call was made and answered.
tips: The system says one thing, the guest says another. Now what?
Is being right the same as being useful here?

items.situation: A regular corporate guest asks for a free upgrade every visit, and always mentions how much his company spends.
tips: Where is your line, and how do you say it without losing the account?

items.situation: A guest posts a one-star review about noise. The noise was a wedding your hotel had confirmed to her in writing.
tips: She was warned. Does that end the conversation?
